_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order). Test 8 mixes inference, reference ('This'), the meaning of a phrase, the writer's purpose, attitude and a final question whose answer links back to the opening ('all right'). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 8.
title: All right, actually
subtitle: Nell Garvey left one of the country's most admired restaurant kitchens to cook lunch for a primary school. Tom Fairley spent a lunchtime with her.

cards.text: At twenty to twelve, Nell Garvey is standing over a pot of gravy large enough to bath a small dog in, tasting it from a plastic spoon. Two years ago she was second-in-command at Marlowe's, a restaurant where diners book months ahead and the reviews are written by people who use words like 'sublime'. Now she cooks for four hundred and twenty pupils at Fernhill Primary School, and her harshest critics are seven years old. 'At Marlowe's, nobody ever said the food was just all right,' she tells me. 'Here, all right is the best review you'll get. I'm still working towards it.'
cards.question: What does Nell suggest about the people she cooks for now?
choices: They are harder to please than her customers used to be.
They complain more about the food than adults do.
They prefer the kind of food served at Marlowe's.
They are more polite about her cooking than critics were.
cards.highlight: Here, all right is the best review you'll get. I'm still working towards it.
cards.why: Even 'all right' is 'the best review you'll get', and she is 'still working towards it', so the children are tougher critics than Marlowe's diners. Nothing says they complain (B) or are polite (D).

cards.text: Her move surprised almost everyone she knew. The head chef at Marlowe's, she says, assumed she was joking and then assumed she was ill. The truth was simpler. Her nephew had shown her a photograph of his school lunch: a grey piece of fish, some pale chips and a spoonful of peas. 'He wasn't complaining,' she says. 'That was the worst part. He thought that was just what lunch was.' This, more than any argument about healthy eating, was what made her apply for the job at Fernhill when it was advertised a few weeks later.
cards.question: What does 'This' refer to in 'This, more than any argument about healthy eating, was what made her apply'?
choices: the head chef's reaction to her decision
the poor quality of the fish in the photograph
her nephew's belief that a poor meal was normal
an argument she had had about healthy eating
cards.highlight: He thought that was just what lunch was.
cards.why: 'The worst part' was that he 'wasn't complaining': he thought a poor lunch was normal. B is tempting, but the fish alone is not what she says upset her; D twists 'more than any argument', which mentions no real argument.

cards.text: The first term, she admits, was humbling. She arrived with a notebook full of ambitious menus and discovered that she had a budget of ninety pence a child, a kitchen designed in the 1970s and forty minutes to feed everyone. Her first new dish, a Moroccan-style chicken with apricots, came back almost untouched. 'I'd been cooking for myself, really,' she says. 'Showing off.' So she started again, and this time she began by asking the children. Their requests were not what she expected: soup, mostly, and anything they were allowed to put together themselves.
cards.question: What does Nell mean when she says she had been 'cooking for myself'?
choices: She ended up eating the dishes the children refused.
She had chosen dishes to display her skill rather than to suit the children.
She was not used to cooking in such large quantities.
She had been given no help in the school kitchen.
cards.highlight: 'I'd been cooking for myself, really,' she says. 'Showing off.'
cards.why: 'Showing off' explains the phrase: the menus were about her ability, not the pupils, which is why she then 'began by asking the children'. A takes the words literally; C and D are difficulties nobody mentions.

cards.text: Which is how Fernhill came to have what the children call 'the building station'. At half past twelve I watch a queue of eight-year-olds assemble their own wraps from bowls of grated carrot, beans, rice and chicken, with the concentration of surgeons. One boy constructs something so large that it has to be eaten with a knife and fork, and he is visibly proud of it. A dinner lady tells me that plates used to come back half full. Now, she says, the bins are so light that the caretaker asked whether the school had lost some pupils.
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the caretaker's question?
choices: to show that the caretaker had not been told about the changes
to suggest that the number of pupils had fallen
to criticise the size of the portions
to show, with humour, how much less food is now thrown away
cards.highlight: the bins are so light that the caretaker asked whether the school had lost some pupils
cards.why: Plates 'used to come back half full'; now the bins are so light the caretaker jokes about missing pupils, so waste has fallen. B takes the joke literally; the huge wrap is a source of pride, not criticism (C).

cards.text: Does she miss Marlowe's? She takes a long time to answer. She misses the precision, she says, and the people, and sometimes the excitement of a Saturday night with every table full. What she does not miss is cooking for people she never saw. 'At Marlowe's the plates went through a door and that was it. Here I can see who's eating the soup and who's hiding the broccoli under a napkin.' She says this with the satisfaction of a detective rather than the irritation of a cook, and makes a note of the boy's name.
cards.question: How does Nell feel about her old job now?
choices: She regrets leaving it and would like to go back.
She did not get on with the people she worked with.
She values parts of it but prefers being able to see her diners.
She found the pressure of busy evenings too much.
cards.highlight: What she does not miss is cooking for people she never saw.
cards.why: She misses 'the precision… the people… the excitement', but not 'cooking for people she never saw'. B contradicts 'the people'; D contradicts missing the Saturday excitement; nothing suggests she wants to return (A).

cards.text: As the last class leaves, a girl of about seven stops at the hatch, where Nell is wiping down the counter. She looks at the empty soup bowls for a moment, like a critic studying a menu, and announces that today's lunch was 'all right, actually'. Then she runs off to the playground. Nell says nothing, but she writes something in the notebook she keeps in her apron pocket, and for the rest of the afternoon she looks like someone who has just been given a glowing review in a national newspaper. Which, in a way, she has.
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest about Nell?
choices: She has received the kind of praise she said she was working towards.
She is disappointed that the girl's comment was not more positive.
She is planning to write about the school for a newspaper.
She cares more about adults' opinions than children's.
cards.why: 'All right' takes us back to the first paragraph, where she called it 'the best review you'll get'; her reaction shows she treats it as a glowing review. B misreads 'all right'; the newspaper is only a comparison (C).
